title: How We Learned About the Body
objective: After this level you can describe how dissection and microscopes revealed the body's inner workings.
summary: Galen's anatomy came from animals. In 1543 Vesalius dissected humans himself. Microscopes let Hooke name cells (1665) and Leeuwenhoek see bacteria (1683).

cards.headline: For centuries, doctors learned human anatomy from apes and pigs.
cards.body: Europe's most trusted anatomy books came from Galen, a Greek physician in the Roman Empire, who couldn't dissect human bodies. His books were still the standard in the 1500s. Two new ways of looking changed that: opening up the human body, and magnifying it.

cards.headline: Vesalius looked for himself
cards.body: In 1543, Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body, built on human dissections he did with his own hands. It was more accurate than any description before it, and it caught Galen's slips. Galen had said the human lower jaw is two bones. That's true for a dog. In people, it's one.

events.label: Vesalius's book maps the body from human dissection
Robert Hooke names 'cells' after the boxes he sees in cork
Leeuwenhoek describes bacteria from his own teeth
Schleiden and Schwann: all living things are made of cells

cards.headline: Microbiology began with a set of teeth
cards.body: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single lenses, magnifying up to about 300 times. In 1683 he looked at the plaque from his own teeth and saw 'little animalcules' moving about: bacteria, seen for the first time. The microbes you met in Level 8 had been living on people all along. It took a homemade lens to notice them.

cards.headline: History: traced
learned: Hooke named cells (1665); Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria (1683)
